e.t: Abira, also rendered Avira, is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object, so its basic meaning is the name itself. This name occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus: once in Genesis 25:4 and once in Nehemiah 1:1. The available information does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain the identity or role of either person, but it does establish that Abira is used as a proper name in these two passages.

Agari is a proper name, functioning as the personal designation of someone mentioned in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or general concept; it identifies a particular person by name. This word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 11:38. Since the verse text is not included here, the surrounding passage is needed to explain who Agari was or what role that person held in the account.

This Greek LXX verb means “meditate”: to give sustained, thoughtful attention to something. It describes an active mental practice rather than a passing thought. In the LXX, it occurs 12 times, with most occurrences in Psalms, showing its repeated use for reflective thought in biblical language. The word also appears in Genesis and Sirach, so its meaning is not limited to one book or setting. Its exact force in any verse depends on what the surrounding passage identifies as the subject of meditation.

This word means “thistle,” a noun naming a prickly plant. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Kings 14:9. Its meaning is therefore straightforward at the word level: it identifies the plant itself rather than an action, quality, or person. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain why the plant is mentioned there, but the word’s ordinary lexical sense remains “thistle.”

This noun means “thunderbolt,” referring to a powerful flash or strike associated with a storm. It occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, once in Job and once in Sirach. The word itself identifies the object rather than expressing an action, command, or personal quality. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

This noun means “strength”—the ability, force, or power by which someone can act, endure, or prevail. It names strength as a quality rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it occurs four times, including once in Daniel and three times in the Maccabean books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what person, group, or power the surrounding passage connects with it.

This verb means to adopt foreign customs—that is, to take on practices associated with another people. It describes a deliberate change in customary conduct rather than merely encountering something foreign. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 18:5. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the adoption of customs from outside one’s own people.

This Greek LXX verb means “dim-sighted”: to have impaired or unclear vision. It describes a condition in which someone does not see clearly, rather than naming a person or object. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 1 Kings 12:24. Because the available lexical meaning is brief and the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise force in that passage must be understood from the larger context. Its central idea remains limited or weakened sight.

Ammon is a proper name used for the people or land known as Ammon. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it appears 102 times, beginning in Numbers and continuing through 1 Maccabees. The name is especially frequent in Judges, 2 Samuel, and 1 Chronicles, showing its repeated place in Israel’s historical record. Its normal function is to identify Ammon rather than describe an action or quality.

This verb means to “recline” or “lay” someone or something down. It describes placing a person or object in a resting position, or settling down oneself, depending on the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 3 Maccabees 5:16. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, since the verse text is not included here. Its basic idea remains movement into a laid-back or lying position.

This verb means to roll things up together, describing the act of gathering or folding them into one rolled form. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Ezekiel 2:10. The word expresses a concrete action rather than a general condition or quality. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the combining and rolling up of something together.

This adjective describes someone or something as “trustworthy”—worthy of confidence and dependable. It identifies a person, statement, or matter that can be relied on rather than doubted. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times: twice in Proverbs and once in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense is being worthy of trust.

This Greek LXX verb means “go off” or “go away.” It describes leaving one place, person, or situation and going elsewhere. As a verb, it expresses the action of departing rather than naming the traveler or destination. The word occurs 188 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, so it is a common way to describe movement away. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains departure or going away.

This noun refers to anything cast away—discarded material or refuse. It names what is thrown out because it is no longer wanted or useful, rather than something retained for use. In the Greek Old Testament wording preserved in the Wisdom of Solomon, it occurs twice, both times rendered “refuse.” Its basic sense is therefore concrete and straightforward: something rejected and cast aside. The surrounding verse determines what particular object is being described.

This adjective describes someone or something as “not precipitate”—not acting in a rushed or rash way. It presents restraint rather than sudden action. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 3:14. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is clear: the person or action is not hasty.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “dishonor”: to treat someone as lacking the honor or respect due to them. It describes an action directed toward a person or another honored subject, rather than merely an inward feeling. The word appears 13 times in the Greek Old Testament, across books including 1 Samuel, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Lamentations, and Obadiah. Its exact force in any particular passage is clarified by the surrounding verse and context.

This noun describes someone who is “one’s own master”—a person regarded as having authority over himself rather than being under another master. Its central idea is personal self-rule or self-command. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs five times, all in 4 Maccabees. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine how this idea functions in each passage, but the basic meaning remains one who possesses authority over himself. The word is not merely a title for an external ruler; it points to self-directed mastery.

This adverb means “fearlessly,” describing someone acting without being afraid. It tells how an action is carried out rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Proverbs 1:33. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the word’s basic sense is clear, while its precise force in that verse must be understood from the sentence and passage around it. Its central idea is confident action that is not restrained by fear.

Achinadab is a personal name, referring to a particular man rather than expressing a general idea, action, or quality. The name is also represented as “Akhinathav.” In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Kings 4:14. Because it is a name, its meaning here is primarily identification: it distinguishes this individual from other people mentioned in the surrounding account. The name itself does not provide enough information to describe the man’s character, role, or significance apart from the passage in which he is named.

Baal, also rendered Vaal, is a proper name. It identifies a named figure or object rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs 70 times across 59 verses, from Numbers through Zephaniah. Its repeated appearance in passages involving named places, people, and acts of worship shows that Baal functions as a specific name within the biblical account. The exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Baitheneth, also rendered Vetheneth, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an idea or action. It identifies a named location or entity in the Greek Old Testament tradition, appearing once, in Judges 1:33. Because no surrounding verse text or further lexical definition is available here, the name itself supplies the main meaning: it is the designation of Baitheneth, also known as Vetheneth.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person identified as Banai or Vane. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 15:24. Because the available information gives the name but not the verse text or surrounding context, it does not support further conclusions about this person’s role or significance in that passage. The name itself functions as an individual designation rather than a general description, action, quality, or theological term.

This noun means “wedding,” referring to the marriage celebration or occasion. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, it occurs 11 times, including passages in Genesis, Esther, and Wisdom. Its basic sense centers on the event that marks or celebrates a marriage, rather than on a person or a general feeling. The surrounding verse determines the particular details, but the word consistently points to a wedding occasion.

Gethedan, also given as Yethethan, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It functions as a specific name in the Greek Old Testament, appearing once in the LXX corpus, in Joshua 21:23. Because it is a name, its meaning is primarily identification: it points to the particular person or place named in that passage, while the surrounding verse supplies the details of what is being identified.

This noun means “heifer,” referring to a young female cow. In the Greek Old Testament, it names this kind of animal in ordinary lists and narrative references, including Genesis 15:9 and several offerings recorded in Numbers 7. The word occurs 39 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical material, with most occurrences in the Old Testament portion of the corpus. Its basic meaning remains consistent: a heifer, rather than a person, place, or abstract idea.

“Nourishment” refers to what provides food or sustenance needed to maintain life and strength. This noun names the provision itself rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 6:49. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains the supply that sustains someone’s physical needs.

This Greek LXX verb means “drive”—to cause someone or something to move onward. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Deuteronomy 32:11. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains the active movement of driving or urging forward. This is a rare word in the LXX corpus, with no other recorded occurrence in that corpus.

The word means “glorify.” As a verb, it describes giving glory—recognizing, displaying, or honoring someone’s greatness. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish books, it occurs 121 times, showing that glorifying is a recurring way Scripture speaks about honoring God or acknowledging greatness. Its precise force in a sentence depends on who is glorified and how the surrounding passage presents that action. This Greek LXX word should be understood within that Greek-scriptural corpus.

This adjective describes a place or stronghold that is hard to take by siege. It points to serious resistance against an attacking force, emphasizing how difficult the capture would be. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 2 Maccabees 12:21. The word’s basic sense identifies something difficult for besiegers to conquer, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what place or situation it describes.

This verb means to shut someone or something in, or to close it. It describes an action of confinement or securing something within a space. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Ezekiel 3:24, so its broader range of use is not illustrated by repeated passages. Its central idea remains straightforward: bringing something inside and preventing it from being open or freely outside.

This Greek LXX verb means “roll up” or “enclose.” It describes an action in which something is gathered into a rolled form or surrounded and closed in. As a verb, it expresses what someone or something does rather than naming an object, person, or quality. It occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, once in 2 Kings and once in Isaiah. The precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its description of what is being rolled up or enclosed.

This noun means “shining forth” or “brightness”—the visible radiance or bright appearance of something. It describes light that comes out clearly or makes something noticeable by its brilliance. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 5:3. The word’s central idea is therefore the appearance or expression of brightness, while the surrounding verse determines precisely what is shining and how that brightness functions in context.

Eliasib is a personal name, rendered “Eliasib” or “Eliasiv.” It identifies a person rather than describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, the name occurs seven times across six verses, appearing in genealogical, priestly, and postexilic records. These occurrences span 1 Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah, so the name belongs to several historical settings and may identify more than one person. The name itself does not provide enough information to determine which Eliasib is intended without the surrounding passage.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person called “Emēr” or “Emir.” It does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; it identifies an individual in the Old Testament Greek translation. The name occurs twice in the Greek LXX, in 1 Kings 22:26 and 2 Chronicles 18:25. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative, but its basic function remains that of a personal name.

This word means “banishment”: being forced or ordered to leave a place or community. It is a noun, so it names the condition or act of being sent away rather than describing the person who leaves. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Lamentations 2:14. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains removal from a place or people.

This verb means “applaud”: to express approval or admiration for someone or something. It describes an active response of praise rather than a person, object, or fixed title. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 25 times, showing that it is used across different settings while retaining this central sense. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording and subject.

This verb means “pray”: to address God in prayer. It describes the act of bringing words or requests before God rather than merely thinking or speaking in general. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Deuteronomy and 1 Chronicles. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central meaning remains the act of praying. The word is found in the LXX corpus and should be understood here as a Greek rendering within that Old Testament translation tradition.

This noun means “increase” or “growth”—an expansion in amount, number, or produce. It describes something becoming greater rather than remaining at its former level. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in the Old Testament corpus. It is rendered “increase” in two recorded instances, supporting the central sense of added abundance. The surrounding verse determines what is increasing, but the word itself points to the result or condition of becoming more.

This adjective describes something as “straightforward” or “right.” It can identify what is proper, direct, or correct, depending on the sentence in which it appears. The word occurs 43 times in the LXX corpus, with most occurrences in the Old Testament portion. Its repeated rendering as “right” supports the sense of something fitting or morally proper, while “straightforward” highlights directness rather than complexity. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This noun means “commendation” or “acclamation”: an expressed approval or public affirmation given to someone. It names words or expressions that honor, approve, or celebrate a person or action, rather than describing the person who receives them. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs 91 times across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so it is a recurring term for spoken or expressed approval. Its exact force in a verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This adjective describes someone as “in good cheer,” expressing a cheerful and positive state of mind. It refers to a person or group marked by gladness and encouragement rather than discouragement. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, the word occurs twice, both in 3 Maccabees. Its exact emphasis in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic sense remains a description of cheerful well-being or spirit.

This word means “stew,” a noun naming a prepared dish of cooked food. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs eight times, including passages in Genesis and 2 Kings. Its repeated use in these food-related settings shows that it refers to the dish itself rather than to an action or quality. The precise significance of the stew in any particular verse depends on that passage’s surrounding wording, but the basic meaning remains the same: a cooked dish called stew.

This adjective describes something made with leaven, so that it has fermented or become leavened. It is used for food that is not unleavened. In the Greek Old Testament, the word appears four times, all in Exodus and Leviticus, where it identifies the kind of bread or food being discussed. Its central idea is therefore straightforward: something affected by leaven through fermentation, rather than remaining without it. The exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the food being described.

Etam, also rendered Itam, is a proper name used for a specific biblical designation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Judges 15, appearing in Judges 15:8 and Judges 15:11. Because it is a proper name rather than a common descriptive word, its meaning is primarily its identifying function: it names the same designated entity in those passages. The precise significance of that entity depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “goddess,” referring to a female deity. It names a divine figure understood as feminine rather than using a general word for a god. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Isaiah. Its basic meaning is clear, while the surrounding verse determines what particular goddess or situation is being discussed. This entity belongs to the Greek LXX and should therefore be kept distinct from Greek New Testament word records.

This Greek LXX noun means “heap”—a gathered or piled mass of things. It names something collected together rather than a single separate item. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, in Genesis, Deuteronomy, and Job. Its basic meaning remains simple and concrete; the surrounding verse determines what has been heaped together and why that image matters there.

This word means “daughter”: a female child viewed in relation to her parents. It is a noun used for an individual daughter or, in plural form, several daughters. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 542 times, showing that it is a regular family term across the corpus. It can occur in passages concerning family relationships, inheritance, marriage, and household life, though its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means “arming with breastplates,” referring to the act of equipping people with protective armor. It describes preparation for defense or battle rather than the breastplate itself. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 5:3. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the provision or use of breastplate armor.

This Greek LXX noun means “healing” or “remedy”—something that restores health or provides relief. It refers to the cure or healing effect needed when harm or sickness has occurred, rather than naming the person who heals. The word appears nine times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, including passages in Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Wisdom. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word denotes “12” and is also identified with “lamedh.” It functions as an indeclinable number, so its basic role is to mark or identify twelve rather than describe an action, person, or quality. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, at Psalms 118:89. The supplied information does not provide the surrounding verse text, so the specific purpose of the marking must be understood from that passage’s context.

This word means “clothing” or “clothes”—the garments a person wears. It is a noun used for ordinary items of dress, whether referring to a single garment or clothing in general. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 209 times, showing that it is a normal word for garments across many kinds of passages. Its usage begins in Genesis and continues through the Old Testament books represented in this corpus.

This Greek LXX verb means “strengthen”: to make someone or something stronger, firmer, or more capable. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so its precise force depends on what is being strengthened in the surrounding sentence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 41:7. The available lexical sense is clear even though the verse text is not included here.

Kainaion or Keneon is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament translation. It identifies a named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. The name is given as “Kainaion; Keneon.” It occurs once, in Numbers 24:21, so its exact referent must be understood from that passage. Since the verse text and surrounding context are not provided here, no more specific identification can be stated safely.

This noun means “holding,” referring to something kept or held. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 67 times, so it is used across a range of passages rather than describing only one special situation. Its occurrences extend from Genesis through the later biblical writings, with frequent use in Ezekiel, Leviticus, and Numbers. The surrounding verse determines whether the word emphasizes the act of holding or the thing held.

This adjective describes someone who is downcast, especially with the eyes lowered. It points to an outward posture or appearance marked by a subdued, downcast gaze. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Wisdom 17:4, so its use is uncommon in this corpus. The surrounding verse is needed to determine the precise reason or significance of that downcast appearance.

This noun refers to an “empty tomb” or “cenotaph,” a tomb or memorial associated with no body. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Samuel 19. The word identifies a burial place by its empty condition rather than describing a person, action, or emotion. Its precise significance in either reference depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains a tomb that is empty or serves as an empty memorial.

This Greek LXX noun means a stringed instrument, specifically a lyre. It refers to an instrument used to produce music, especially in settings involving musicians, singing, or worship. The word occurs 22 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented in this corpus, showing a recurring musical meaning rather than a figurative one. Its precise use in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains a lyre or similar stringed instrument.

This verb means “doze” or “fall asleep.” It describes the act of entering sleep or being asleep, rather than expressing a particular emotion or spiritual condition. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it is used broadly for ordinary sleep. The word occurs 192 times in this LXX corpus, from Genesis through the Epistle of Jeremiah, showing that it is a common term for sleeping. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage.

This word means “pool,” referring to a contained body or gathering place of water. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament for pools mentioned in descriptions of places and works. The word occurs ten times in the Greek Old Testament, across Isaiah, Nehemiah, 2 Kings, Ecclesiastes, and Nahum. Its ordinary sense remains concrete: a pool or pools of water, rather than a person, action, or spiritual quality. The surrounding verse determines which particular pool is intended.

This verb means “peel off”: to remove an outer covering or layer from something. It describes a physical action rather than a person, object, or abstract idea. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Scriptures represented here, appearing in Genesis and 1 Maccabees. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what covering or surface is being removed, but its central meaning remains the act of stripping something away.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Magdō” or “Magtho.” It identifies a particular named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at 1 Kings 2:35. Because the available lexical information gives only the name and does not include the verse text, its specific identity and role must be determined from the surrounding passage rather than from the word alone.

Makeda, also given as Makitha, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times, all within seven verses of Joshua, from Joshua 10:10 through Joshua 12:16. The name identifies the same named subject wherever it appears, while the surrounding verse determines what is being said about it. Its meaning is therefore best understood as the proper name “Makeda; Makitha,” not as a general vocabulary term.

This word is the proper name “Maraiōth,” also given as “Mareoth.” It functions as a personal name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 9:11. The name itself does not provide a broader descriptive meaning; its role is to identify the individual associated with that name in the passage.

Maōnim, also rendered Maonim, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a specific biblical name, but the available information does not establish whether it refers to a person, family, place, or group. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 2:50. Its precise referent must therefore be understood from the surrounding passage rather than from the name alone.

This proper noun identifies something as “Mēdian” or “Mithian.” It is a name or designation rather than a general descriptive word. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Maccabees, at 1 Maccabees 8:8 and 14:1. The exact reference of the name in either passage depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here.

This Greek LXX noun refers to a “teller of legends” or “romancer”—someone who recounts legendary or invented stories. It describes a person by the kind of stories he tells, rather than naming a physical object or an action. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Baruch 3:23. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context, which is not included here.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Nagargasnaser” or “Nagargaznaser,” rather than a term describing an action, quality, or object. Its role is to identify a particular named entity in the Greek Old Testament wording. It occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Jeremiah 46:3. Because no verse text or surrounding context is included here, the name’s specific referent cannot be described further; its lexical function is simply that of a proper name.

This word means “young bird” or “nestling,” referring to a bird that is still young and dependent. It is a noun, so it names the creature itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 14:15. The word’s basic meaning is clear from its direct definition, while the precise force of the reference depends on the surrounding verse and passage. It describes a young bird in ordinary, concrete language.

Nooma is a proper name, referring to a person named Nooma rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Chronicles chapter 8. Because the available information identifies the name but does not provide the surrounding verse text, its specific family or narrative role cannot be explained here. The name itself carries the straightforward meaning “Nooma.”

This word means “wine,” referring to the fermented drink made from grapes. It is a noun used for wine as an ordinary drink and as something presented or used in various settings. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 214 times, showing that it is a well-established term throughout this corpus. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: wine itself, rather than a person, action, or abstract idea.

e.h: A Large Bird or Bird of Prey
e.t: This noun refers to a large bird, especially a bird of prey. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in the LXX of Numbers 24:1. The word identifies a kind of bird rather than expressing an action or quality. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is straightforward: a large bird or predatory bird.

This verb means to lament or wail—to express deep sorrow aloud. It describes an outward cry of grief rather than a quiet feeling alone. The word appears three times in the LXX, all in deuterocanonical books, so its basic meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not provided here. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on who is grieving and what has caused the lament.

This adverb means “nowhere,” referring to no place at all. It is used to state that something cannot be found, does not exist, or is absent in any location, with the surrounding sentence determining the exact force. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, in passages from 1 Kings, Job, and Proverbs. Its basic sense remains straightforward: it excludes every possible place rather than identifying one particular location.

This word means “crowd” or “mass,” referring to a group of people gathered together. It is a noun used for a collective body rather than for one individual. In the LXX corpus, it occurs 45 times across 42 verses, showing that it is a recurring term for groups of people in different settings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a crowd or mass.

This noun refers to the whole household—the complete group of people belonging to a home or family. It can describe a household as a unit rather than focusing on one individual member. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including passages in Genesis, Exodus, Esther, and 3 Maccabees. Its central sense remains collective: everyone included within the household. The surrounding verse determines precisely which people are included in each occurrence.

This noun means “consolation”: comfort or encouragement given to someone who needs strengthening. It names the help that eases sorrow, distress, or discouragement rather than describing a person or event. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice—once in Esther and once in Wisdom. Its precise emphasis in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains consolation offered or received.

This word means “of a virgin,” describing a person or thing in relation to a virgin. It functions as an adjective and can also be used as a noun, so its role may be either descriptive or identifying. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Esther and once in Joel. Its precise use in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains centered on a virgin.

This Greek LXX verb means “hungry”: it describes experiencing a need or desire for food. It is used for people who lack nourishment or are seeking something to eat. The word occurs 44 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, including passages from Genesis, Psalms, Proverbs, and Isaiah. Its basic meaning remains straightforward, while the surrounding verse determines whether the word simply describes physical hunger or contributes to a broader statement about a person’s condition. The supplied references include Genesis 41:55, Psalms 106:9, and Proverbs 6:30.

This noun means “broad space”—an open or widened place rather than a narrow, confined one. It can describe the condition or setting of having room to move freely. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs six times: five times in Old Testament books and once in Sirach. Its central idea remains the same wherever it appears: spaciousness, room, or an expanded place. The surrounding verse determines how that idea functions in each passage.

“Floating” describes something that remains on the surface or is carried along rather than sinking. It is an adjective, so it identifies an object or thing by this quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, the word appears twice, making it an uncommon term in this corpus. Its basic sense stays focused on being afloat or moving while supported by water or another surface.

This noun means “buckle-pin,” a small fastening piece associated with a buckle. It names a physical object rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in 1 Maccabees. The word’s precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic meaning remains a buckle-pin or similar fastening part. This adjective describes someone who is meek—gentle, humble, and not driven by harshness or self-assertion. It presents meekness as a settled character rather than merely a quiet moment or outward manner. In the Greek Septuagint, this word appears twice, both times in Proverbs, where its meaning belongs to the wisdom teaching of that book. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains a restrained and humble disposition.
